Spring Boot Auto-Configuration

How Auto-Configuration Works

Auto-configuration is driven by a fixed loading sequence: @SpringBootApplication includes @EnableAutoConfiguration , which activates AutoConfigurationImportSelector . @SpringBootApplication as Entry Point

@SpringBootApplication is a composed annotation that combines @SpringBootConfiguration , @EnableAutoConfiguration , and @ComponentScan . AutoConfigurationImportSelector

AutoConfigurationImportSelector implements DeferredImportSelector and is the class responsible for reading the list of auto-configuration candidates. In Spring Boot 3 it reads META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports (one fully-qualified class name per line).
Auto-Configuration Ordering

Auto-configuration classes can declare ordering constraints using @AutoConfigureBefore and @AutoConfigureAfter to control which configurations are processed first. @Conditional Annotations

Spring Boot ships a rich set of @Conditional annotations that allow auto-configuration classes to declare precisely when they should apply. All of these annotations can be placed on @Configuration classes or individual @Bean methods. When multiple conditions are present, all must pass for the config
@ConditionalOnClass

Matches when the specified class (or all specified classes) are present on the classpath. This is the most common condition in auto-configurations — it ensures that a driver or library class exists before registering beans that depend on it. The check is done at the bytecode level without actually l
@ConditionalOnMissingBean

Matches when no bean of the specified type (or name) has been registered yet in the application context. This is the primary mechanism that lets users override auto-configured beans — by declaring their own bean of the same type, they suppress the auto-configuration's bean silently. When used withou
@ConditionalOnProperty

Matches based on the value of a Spring Environment property. You can require the property to exist ( matchIfMissing = false , the default) or to have a specific value. The havingValue attribute enables matching only when the property equals a particular string. This is the standard way to make a fea
@ConditionalOnWebApplication

Matches when the application is a web application. You can restrict to a specific web application type using type = Type.SERVLET (traditional blocking Spring MVC) or type = Type.REACTIVE (Spring WebFlux). The default matches either. Web auto-configurations like DispatcherServletAutoConfiguration use
@ConditionalOnExpression

Matches when a SpEL (Spring Expression Language) expression evaluates to true . This is the most flexible — and most expensive — condition because the expression is evaluated at runtime. @ConditionalOnBean

Matches when at least one bean of the specified type or name is already registered in the context. This is the inverse of @ConditionalOnMissingBean . A common pattern is to declare additional infrastructure beans (metrics adapters, health indicators) only when the primary service bean already exists
@ConditionalOnSingleCandidate

Matches when exactly one bean of the specified type exists in the context, or when multiple candidates exist but one is marked @Primary . This is especially useful in reactive vs. blocking scenarios where a configuration should activate only when there is an unambiguous primary candidate, rather tha
@ConditionalOnNotWebApplication

Matches only when the application is not a web application — the complement of @ConditionalOnWebApplication . @ConditionalOnJava

Matches based on the JVM version at runtime. You specify a range using JavaVersion enum constants and a range attribute ( EQUAL_OR_NEWER or OLDER_THAN ). This allows library authors to provide different implementation strategies depending on which language features are available, without branching a
@ConditionalOnResource

Matches when a specific resource (file, classpath entry) is present. The resource location uses the standard Spring resource syntax: classpath: , file: , etc. This is useful for auto-configurations that need a configuration file (such as a logback.xml ) to be present before they activate their defau
@ConditionalOnCloudPlatform

Matches when the application is running on a specific cloud platform. Spring Boot detects platforms like CLOUD_FOUNDRY , HEROKU , SAP , and KUBERNETES by inspecting environment variables. If an auto-configuration is activating when you do not want it to, you can exclude it explicitly using the exclude attribute of @SpringBootApplication , or via the spring.autoconfigure.exclude property. Step 2 — The starter Module

Create a second Maven module named my-feature-spring-boot-starter . Step 4 — Consuming the Starter

5. Spring Boot DevTools — Hot Reload

DevTools monitors the JVM classpath for changes and triggers a fast restart — not a full JVM restart. It keeps the JVM alive, swaps only the application's own classes (the app classloader), and restarts the Spring context. This typically takes 1–3 seconds vs 5–20 seconds for a cold start.

<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-devtools</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
    <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>
application.properties

# Enable classpath watcher and restart on change
spring.devtools.restart.enabled=true
